title: A 250-Year-Old Mystery Solved: DNA Finds a Revolutionary War Soldier's Family
summary: Have you ever dug up something old in your backyard and wondered who it belonged to? Now imagine finding a whole skeleton from the American Revolution! In 2022, archaeologists in South Carolina uncovered the remains of 14 soldiers who died in the Battle of Camden in 1780. One of them was just a teenager when he joined the army. His name was John Pumphrey. Using DNA from his bones, scientists matched him to living relatives—about 20,000 of them! One is Nancy White, a 71-year-old woman from Maryland. She was shocked to learn that Pumphrey was her fourth great uncle. Her family had studied their history for years, but they never thought they were related to a soldier because the Pumphreys were Quakers, a religious group that doesn't believe in fighting. But John lost his parents young and joined the army as a home. He fought in famous battles like Brandywine and Valley Forge before a British musket ball killed him at Camden. The graves were super shallow—only about 14 inches deep—because prisoners of war had to dig them with their bare hands. Now, Pumphrey is the oldest unknown person ever identified with genetic genealogy. And the scientist leading the project? She found out she's related to another soldier from the same battlefield!
why_it_matters: This shows that even people from long ago can still have family alive today, and science can uncover stories that remind us how history is personal and exciting.

background_read: The Battle of Camden was a fight in 1780 during the American Revolution, where British soldiers defeated American troops in South Carolina.
Genetic genealogy has helped solve many mysteries, from finding unknown soldiers to helping police solve old crimes.
Quakers are a Christian group that began in England and believe strongly in nonviolence and peace.
Article_Structure: WHO: John Pumphrey, a teenage soldier in the American Revolution, and Nancy White, his living relative.
WHAT: Scientists used DNA from his bones to identify him and connect him to about 20,000 living relatives.
WHERE: The remains were found at the Battle of Camden site in South Carolina.
WHY: The discovery solved a 250-year mystery about who the unknown soldier was and gave his story back to his family.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled because it brings history to life and honors a soldier who was forgotten for centuries. It fills in pieces of family trees.

perspectives.perspective: Some people cautious about using old DNA
perspectives.description: They worry about whether it's right to take DNA from bones without the person's permission, even though it's for learning about the past.
They see this as a huge breakthrough because it's the oldest unknown person ever identified using genetic genealogy, which can help identify many more unknown remains from wars.
